messages.content:
Hey all, we are building an open source RAG bot for this server to answer questions using our ~6 years of chat history. I am looking for TPMs to help build it!
We are going to turn our chat archive into an active knowledge base. From a user perspective, a member will simply ask a question or ping the bot. The bot will instantly reply with a high quality answer sourced directly from past community discussions. Our immediate phase one goal is to tackle the hardest part of the project by extracting and cleaning our 6 year chat backlog.

**How this benefits us**: This eliminates wait times for answers to common technical questions. More importantly, it gives us a practical, hands on AI project to build together and showcase as a community.

**How we’ll work**: We’ll set up a Git repository to manage the architecture, documentation, and code. We are currently looking at a stack utilizing n8n, Gemini, and an open source vector database. This is just a loose starting point and should evolve based on contributor input. We will treat this as a standard open source project where members can own specific pieces of the development pipeline.

**Who this is for**: This is for TPMs who have already built RAG applications and want to help guide the architecture. It is also for TPMs who want to get hands on experience and learn how these systems are actually built.

**Next steps**: If you want to contribute, reply below. I will set up some time in the coming days with everyone who wants to participate to chat about how this effort will work. I will follow up later with the specific platform we will use to coordinate our tasks

A reaction could mean someone engaged positively — agreement, thanks, "lol," acknowledgment — not that the answer was correct. Reactions also skew toward whatever was visible: older messages had years to accumulate them, busy threads and prominent members get more, and most messages have zero. @ThinkInSystems we'll need your help in writing design docs for the following before I can start working on the n8n pipeline: 

1. Retrieval Contract
n8n needs a clear contract for querying Qdrant.
- Query text format
- Embedding model and prefix: search_query:
- Top K, likely top_k=20 initial retrieval
- Final context count, likely deduped/reranked down to 5
- Whether retrieval searches all channels by default
- Metadata filters allowed: channel, thread, date
- Dedupe strategy for overlapping chunks
- Minimum score threshold
- Behavior when results are weak
This is critical. Without it, n8n will retrieve “some chunks,” but not necessarily the right context.

2. Context Assembly Contract
We need to define exactly what context gets sent to the LLM.
For each retrieved chunk, should the prompt include:
- Channel
- Thread name
- Start/end timestamp
- Authors
- Score
 - Raw text
-  Message IDs
- Link back to Discord, if constructible
Also: how many tokens do we allow for retrieved context? What happens if context is too large?

3. Prompt / Response Contract
The bot needs a stable answer policy.
Define:
- Required system prompt
- Required refusal text
- Source/citation style
- Whether to mention uncertainty
- Whether to say “based on TPM Unite history”
- Whether to include channel/thread references
- Whether to invite members to continue discussion
- Safety rule: do not answer beyond retrieved context
This is probably the most important human-facing contract.

messages.content:
- RAG alone is good at evidence retrieval but weak at long-term synthesis. It can find five relevant chunks, but it does not remember that we have already seen this topic many times and that some claims conflict.
- Wiki alone is good at synthesis but risky as a source of truth. If the wiki says “Meta partnership interviews are soft interviews,” we still need raw source evidence behind that claim.

I think there's a place for a hybrid approach: 
 question
-> retrieve Discord chunks-> rerank-> dedupe
-> retrieve relevant wiki pages 
-> cross-check wiki claims against raw discord evidence to ensure it's not hallucinating 
-> Gemini generates balanced answer

Here's a retrospective on the progress we've made so far: 
Phase 0: runtime foundation is up.
Phase 1: transaction spine exists.
Phase 2: active-call happy path works.
Phase 3/3B: observability exists, with Phoenix + Postgres instrumentation.

@CaliMan @Shilpi Got some time to go over all the candidates — final diagnosis, no threshold guessing needed:

RQ-010, RQ-014 — confirmed corpus gap on the specific angle asked. Channel filter works correctly (20/20, 18/20 scoped to #tpm-tradecraft). General dependency management content exists and scores reasonably, but nothing specifically addresses 'remote teams' (RQ-010) or specific tooling/software (RQ-014). Reranker is scoring correctly given what's actually retrieved. Recommend rewriting these questions to match real corpus content, or accepting as known gaps per the Issue #27 pattern.

RQ-012 — confirmed reranker/gate interaction, not a corpus gap. Found a near perfect match in #tpm-stories (score 6.46), literally the same question asked and answered by the community. But everything else falls off a cliff below -3.5. The min 3 candidates rule is correctly blocking a single strong source from answering alone, by design, to prevent thin evidence answers. This isn't a scoring bug, it's the minimum evidence rule doing its job against a topic the corpus only covers once.

Full sweep summary across all 7 false_refusals:
RQ-019, RQ-024 → threshold calibration fix available, but only at the extreme safe edge (-0.0986, set by RQ-039's correct refusal as the ceiling)
RQ-010, RQ-014 → corpus gap on specific question angle, not a system bug
RQ-012 → single strong match blocked by the 3 candidate minimum evidence rule, working as designed
RQ-022, RQ-026 → broad subjective questions, likely no single strong source exists; candidates for relabeling

None of these look like genuine pipeline bugs. They're either real corpus coverage gaps, the minimum evidence rule doing exactly what it's supposed to, or eval cases that may need rewriting to match what the community actually discussed.
